headline: High risk of prompt-injection and data leakage if OpenHands ingests content from the prompt-listing repo into its writable, networked runtime.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Profile A is a content-writing prompt repository with no runtime isolation, while profile B can read/write files, use MCP, and run browsers in a shared runtime. If A’s prompt content is copied into B’s workspace or MCP flow, B may treat attacker-controlled text as instructions. The pathway is plausible but not documented directly, so I choose medium.
conditions: IF content from agent_a is copied into agent_b's workspace or MCP inputs
IF agent_b parses file or web content as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of agent_a content into agent_b
Add a provenance banner to imported prompt files
Require manual review before MCP/browser content is acted on
Use a separate read-only staging folder for agent_a artifacts

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A has no network egress, but agent B has broad egress and reads files in its runtime sandbox. If both share mounted files, B can transmit file contents to external services configured by the user. The shared-workspace pathway is explicit in B’s docs, but A’s side is only a docs-only repository, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF agent_a artifacts are mounted into agent_b's runtime filesystem
IF agent_b sends runtime file contents to its configured model provider or MCP server
mitigations: Keep agent_a artifacts out of agent_b's mounted volume
Use a separate workspace per agent
Restrict agent_b egress for runs touching sensitive files
Review MCP server destinations before enabling them

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent B can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; agent A is non-runnable content. There is no direct write conflict from A, but if A’s files are placed in B’s shared mounted volume, B can overwrite or commit them. Because the shared-volume path is documented only for B and A has no isolation metadata, uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share the same mounted directory
IF agent_b is allowed to modify git state in that directory
mitigations: Mount agent_a content read-only into agent_b
Use separate git worktrees per agent
Disable git writes for runs that only inspect agent_a
Add file-locking around shared directories

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent B can act on browser, shell, and MCP outputs, so if it treats agent A’s prompt content as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream actions. Agent A is a prompt repository rather than a verified fact source, which increases the chance of unverified content being reused. The interaction is inferred, not directly evidenced, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a output as authoritative input
IF agent_b performs shell, browser, or MCP actions based on that output without verification
mitigations: Require a verification step before any action-taking
Label agent_a content as untrusted prompts only
Block direct execution of copied prompt text
Add a human approval gate for downstream actions

E_compliance.rationale: No PHI, residency, or retention mismatch is documented for agent A, and agent B’s profile only states files in the runtime sandbox plus model-provider keys. The pair therefore shows no concrete compliance breach by default; the remaining risk is limited to whatever data the operator mounts. I cite both profiles because the assessment depends on their documented data surfaces.
conditions: IF regulated data is mounted into agent_b's runtime
IF the operator routes that data to a non-compliant external model provider
mitigations: Avoid mounting regulated data into the runtime
Use a compliant provider configuration
Review retention settings before each run
Keep secrets out of prompt repositories
